rights.composition.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
rights.composition.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.
rights.recording.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
rights.recording.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

work.title: Kindertotenlieder

work.version.note: The source identifies the orchestral song, but not its performing edition or editorial alterations. The listening notes use the low-voice orchestral score, C. F. Kahnt plate 4460, for passage-level scoring; they do not claim this exact printed edition was on the performers’ desks. In this transfer, songs IV–V have late pitch-class profiles about a semitone above the written score and the Fischer-Dieskau transfer. The cause—speed, transposition or other processing—has not been established. No tuning correction or numerical tempo comparison is asserted.
performers.note: The Commons description identifies all three performing credits; the independent catalogue corroborates the pairing.
session.date.note: Commons dates the recording to 1950; the day and month remain unestablished. The earlier RCA release catalogue is not used as a session-date source.
session.place.note: The consulted sources do not identify the recording venue. The orchestra’s home city is not used as proof of the session location.
carrier.label.note: Commons names its source as “CD audio RCA”. This is the identified CD source label, not an assertion about the original session medium.
carrier.catalogue.note: No catalogue number identifying the CD used for the Commons upload is supplied. An independent University of the Arts Helsinki catalogue documents an earlier RCA Victor Red Seal LP, LM 1146, with these performers, coupled with Brahms’s Alto Rhapsody; its catalogue date is 1951 and its descriptive release range is 1951–1953. It identifies an earlier issue, not the CD transferred to Commons.
carrier.matrixTakeSides.note: No matrix, take or original side identification is supplied. The absence of those details is not treated as proof that no historical identifiers exist.
transfer.credits.note: The Commons uploader is not treated as a transfer or mastering engineer. No such credit for this particular CD-to-Ogg transfer is identified.
transfer.date.note: No transfer date is supplied; upload dates and historical recording dates are not substituted for it.
transfer.processing.value: Commons provides an uploaded Ogg Vorbis file and an MP3 access derivative.
transfer.processing.note: The embedded Ogg encoder is Xiph.Org libVorbis I 20100325 (Everywhere). The original session medium, earlier mastering, noise reduction and editing history are unestablished. In this transfer, songs IV–V have late pitch-class profiles about a semitone above the written score and the Fischer-Dieskau transfer. The cause—speed, transposition or other processing—has not been established. No tuning correction or numerical tempo comparison is asserted. The analyzed final-song derivative contains approximately twenty seconds at the analysis floor after the closing decay; this is not treated as sustained orchestral sound.
digital.format: MP3 access derivative supplied by Wikimedia Commons; uploaded source: Ogg Vorbis

rights.composition.note: The catalogue gives Mahler’s dates as 1860–1911 and Rückert’s as 1788–1866. This refers to the historical composition and text, not an unidentified modern performing edition; the catalogue’s inconsistent publication year is not adopted.
rights.recording.value: Territorial — Commons applies PD-EU-audio to the sound recording.
rights.recording.note: The template concerns the rights of performers and phonogram producers, not merely the composition. The recording is accepted on that EU territorial basis. United States status and worldwide clearance are not established; no US pre-1926 claim is made.
